media.instructions_for_student: The student will understand that a jump of n steps lands on a number when n is a factor of it, and that the jump sizes reaching every number of a list are its common factors.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Trail Jumper
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S10.T10.C32.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Chapter 13 Animal Jumps, Mowgli's trail and Let Us Do questions 3 to 7 with the lines for jumps of 3, 5 and 10. Practice jump 6 and the pair 20 and 30 (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that a jump of n steps from 0 lands exactly on a number when n is a factor of it, and that the jump sizes that land on every number of a list are the common factors of the list.
- Out of scope: common multiples, prime numbers, finding factors from arrays.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- Mowgli's jungle trail: a winding path of 61 round stones numbered 0 to 60 in four loops (flat drawing). Mowgli sits on stone 0. Eleven friends sit beside their stones as in the book: ant 4, spider 9, frog 12, bird in its nest 14, Kaa the snake 21, Sher Khan the tiger 25, Baloo the bear 30, Akela the wolf 35, deer 39, rabbit 50, monkey 57. A footprint dial under the trail shows the jump size 6 (locked here), and a round green "Go" button sits by Mowgli.
- Instruction line: "Mowgli jumps 6 steps at a time. Which friends will he meet? Tap them."
- The child taps the friends they think he will meet, then presses "Go".
2. Scene and Objects
- Trail: big stone numbers; friends two stones wide; a friend Mowgli lands on lights up with a name tag. Dial: minus, the size, plus (1 to 30).
- Flags: a tap on a stone plants a blue flag (a target), a second tap removes it; at most 2, except where the book's numbers are flagged for the child.
- Common factors board (from Activity 2): a wooden board under the trail; a size that lands on every flag is added in order. Goal chip at the top left of the stage.
3. Main Interaction
- Set the size, press "Go": Mowgli hops from 0, one jump every half second, leaving footprints, and stops when the next jump would pass 60. Each flag then shows a green tick if he landed on it, or a grey ring with the two stones he landed on either side if he skipped it.
- Tap a friend to ring them as a guess; tap again to remove.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" (clears footprints, flags, board) and one that reads "Check", then "Next" when the goal chip is green.
- A guess is never marked wrong. If it differs from the result the strip says, for example, "You guessed the spider. Let us see where he lands."
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Mowgli jumps 6 steps at a time. Which friends will he meet? Tap them." Goal chip: "Meet the friends". Setup: dial locked at 6. Guess: tap friends to ring them, then "Go". Result: footprints on 6, 12, ..., 60; the frog and Baloo light up. Why: "12 = 6 × 2 and 30 = 6 × 5, so jumps of 6 land on the frog and on Baloo. He jumps over the others." Help: guided, each landing shows its label, for example "6 × 2 = 12".
- Activity 2 (independent). Goal line: "Which jump sizes reach both 20 and 30?" Goal chip: "Common factors of 20 and 30". Setup: flags on 20 and 30; dial free. Guess: tap 3, 4 or 5 for a size you think reaches both; then try sizes with "Go". Result: the board holds 1, 2, 5 and 10. Why: "5 × 4 = 20 and 5 × 6 = 30, 10 × 2 = 20 and 10 × 3 = 30. A jump of 4 reaches 20 but skips 30: it lands on 28 and then 32." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal chip: "Jumps of 2, 3, 5 and 10". Four rounds, dial locked at 2, 3, 5, 10. The book's questions: (1) "Mowgli's friends live along the trail on the marked places below. Which of his friends will he be able to visit, if he jumps by 2 steps starting from 0?" (2) "Which of his friends will he be able to meet if he jumps by 3 steps? 3 is a common factor of the numbers ___." (3) "Which numbers will he touch if he jumps by 5 steps? ___. 5 is a common factor of the numbers ___." (4) "Which numbers will he touch if he jumps by 10 steps? ___. 10 is a common factor of the numbers ___." Guess: ring the friends you expect; in rounds 3 and 4 also tap how many numbers he touches (6, 12 or 15; then 3, 6 or 10). Result: 2 meets the ant 4, frog 12, bird 14, Baloo 30, rabbit 50. 3 meets the spider 9, frog 12, Kaa 21, Baloo 30, deer 39, monkey 57. 5 touches 5, 10, ..., 60 (12 numbers) and meets Sher Khan 25, Baloo 30, Akela 35, rabbit 50. 10 touches 10, 20, ..., 60 (6 numbers) and meets Baloo 30, rabbit 50. The blanks fill from the footprints and lit friends. Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line (the book's question): "Let us find some common factors of the numbers 24 and 36. Note that all jumps in the following questions start from 0." Goal chip: "24 and 36". Setup: flags on 24 and 36. Round 1, parts (a) to (c): "Can we jump by 2 steps at a time to reach both 24 and 36?" then 3, then 4 steps. Guess: "Yes" or "No" before "Go". Result: yes each time. Round 2, parts (d) and (e): "What other jumps can we take to reach both 24 and 36?" and "How many common factors can you find for 24 and 36? List them." Dial free. Guess: tap 4, 6 or 8 for how many. The child tries sizes until the board holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Why: "6 × 4 = 24 and 6 × 6 = 36. 12 × 2 = 24 and 12 × 3 = 36. There are 6 common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12." Round 3, part (f): "What about jumping by 1 step each time to reach both 24 and 36?" Guess "Yes" or "No"; result yes. Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal chip: "12 and 13, then jumps of 4". Part 1 (the book's question): "What are the common factors of 12 and 13?" Setup: flags on 12 and 13; dial free. Guess: tap 1, 2 or 3 for how many. Result: the board holds only 1. Why: "12 and 13 have only 1 in common. A jump of 3 reaches 12 but then lands on 15, so it skips 13." Part 2 (the book's question): "Find which of the following numbers can be reached by jumps of 4 steps? 4 is the common factor of the numbers ___." Setup: flags on 10, 16, 27, 36, 48; dial locked at 4. Guess: tap the flags you expect to be reached, then "Go". Result: 16, 36 and 48 get ticks and drop into the blank. Why: "16 = 4 × 4, 36 = 4 × 9 and 48 = 4 × 12, but 4 skips 10 (8 then 12) and 27 (24 then 28)." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line (the book's question): "Find the common factors of the following pairs of numbers." Goal chip: "Pairs (a) to (i)". Setup: nine pairs, one at a time, both flagged. Guess: tap 1, 2 or 3 for how many common factors. The child tries sizes until the board is full. Result: (a) 12 and 16: 1, 2, 4; (b) 8 and 12: 1, 2, 4; (c) 4 and 16: 1, 2, 4; (d) 2 and 9: 1; (e) 3 and 5: 1; (f) 12 and 15: 1, 3; (g) 20 and 5: 1, 5; (h) 9 and 21: 1, 3; (i) 6 and 27: 1, 3. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A jump of n steps from 0 lands on the multiples of n, so it lands on a number exactly when n goes into it: n is a factor of the number. A jump that skips a number lands on a stone each side of it.
- A size that lands on every flag is a common factor; the biggest is not the only one, and 1 always works.
- Rules: "A jump of n lands on a number only if n goes into it exactly." "A common factor reaches every number in the list." "1 is a common factor of every pair."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: a green tick on the flag, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong: a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line. Retry is free.
- Mistake: says a jump reaches a number it jumps over, for example 4 and 30 -> "4 lands on 28 and then on 32. It jumps over 30, so it does not reach it." Stones 28 and 32 pulse.
- Mistake: stops at the biggest common factor -> on Check: "There are 2 more jump sizes that reach both." The empty slots pulse. Forgets 1 -> "A jump of 1 lands on every stone. 1 is a common factor too."
- Mistake: taps a skipped friend, for example the spider for jumps of 2 -> "2 lands on 8 and then on 10. It skips 9."
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) words: "Count in jumps from 0. Does Mowgli land exactly on the number, or jump over it?" (2) visual: faint footprints of the current size appear and every flag or friend on a footprint glows green. (3) almost the answer: for 24 and 36 "2 × 12 = 24 and 2 × 18 = 36, so 2 reaches both. 3 × 8 = 24 and 3 × 12 = 36, so 3 does too. Now try 4, 6 and 12."
- Edge cases: a jump of 1 reaches every number; a jump of 30 lands only on 30 and 60; when one flag is a multiple of the other (20 and 5) the smaller number is a common factor; numbers that follow each other (12 and 13) share only 1.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result is on screen (four rounds; the full boards; 16, 36, 48 in the blank).
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A jump of n lands on a number only if n goes into it exactly." "A common factor reaches every number in the list." "1 is a common factor of every pair of numbers." Think and talk: "What do you notice about the common factors of different pairs of numbers?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: winding trail of 61 numbered stones (code-drawn); Mowgli and the eleven friends (flat drawings, as in the book); blue flags, footprints, ticks (code-drawn); wooden board. Language: English.

content.text:
Worked example: Mowgli jumps 4 steps at a time from 0. Which of the places 8, 14, 20 and 26 can he land on? What can you say about 4 and the places he lands on?
1. His landing places are the multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28.
2. 8 is on the list: 4 × 2 = 8, so he lands on 8 after 2 jumps.
3. 14 is not on the list: he lands on 12 and then on 16, so he skips 14.
4. 20 is on the list: 4 × 5 = 20, so he lands on 20 after 5 jumps.
5. 26 is not on the list: he lands on 24 and then on 28, so he skips 26.
6. 4 divides 8 and 20 completely, so 4 is a common factor of 8 and 20.
7. Check: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, both exact.
Answer: He lands on 8 and 20, and skips 14 and 26. 4 is a common factor of 8 and 20

content.text:
Worked example: Find the common factors of 18 and 30, and say which jump sizes reach both numbers.
1. List the factors of 18 from its arrays 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
2. List the factors of 30 from its arrays 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30.
3. Pick the numbers that are in both lists: 1, 2, 3 and 6.
4. Each of these is a jump size that lands on both 18 and 30. Jumps of 6 land on 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. Jumps of 9 land on 18 but skip 30: 9, 18, 27, 36.
5. 1 is always a common factor, because a jump of 1 lands on every number.
6. Check: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 30 ÷ 6 = 5, both exact.
Answer: The common factors of 18 and 30 are 1, 2, 3 and 6

Check: 12 × 2 = 24 and 12 × 3 = 36, so 12, the biggest common factor, reaches both. content.text: Mowgli's friends live along the trail on the marked places below. Which of his friends will he be able to visit, if he jumps by $2$ steps starting from $0$?
content.q_figure: A winding trail of numbered stones from 0 to 60 with Mowgli at 0 and his friends at these places: the ant at 4, the spider at 9, the frog at 12, the bird at 14, Kaa the snake at 21, Sher Khan the tiger at 25, Baloo the bear at 30, Akela the wolf at 35, the deer at 39, the rabbit at 50 and the monkey at 57.

content.publication_text: Mowgli's friends live along the trail on the marked places below. Which of his friends will he be able to visit, if he jumps by $2$ steps starting from $0$?

content.text:
1. Jumps of $2$ from $0$ land on $2$, $4$, $6$, $8$ and so on: the even numbers, the multiples of $2$.
2. The friends live at these places: ant $4$, spider $9$, frog $12$, bird $14$, Kaa $21$, Sher Khan $25$, Baloo $30$, Akela $35$, deer $39$, rabbit $50$, monkey $57$.
3. $4 = 2 \times 2$, $12 = 2 \times 6$, $14 = 2 \times 7$, $30 = 2 \times 15$ and $50 = 2 \times 25$, so a jump of $2$ lands on all five of these places.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
4. $9$, $21$, $25$, $35$, $39$ and $57$ are odd numbers, so jumps of $2$ skip them.
5. Mowgli can visit the ant, the frog, the bird, Baloo and the rabbit. $2$ is a common factor of $4$, $12$, $14$, $30$ and $50$.
6. Check: $30 \div 2 = 15$ and $50 \div 2 = 25$, both exact.
Answer: The ant $(4)$, frog $(12)$, bird $(14)$, Baloo $(30)$ and rabbit $(50)$: $2$ is a common factor of $4$, $12$, $14$, $30$ and $50$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. $(a)$: $2 \times 12 = 24$ and $2 \times 18 = 36$, so jumps of $2$ reach both. Yes, $2$ is a common factor of $24$ and $36$.
2. $(b)$: $3 \times 8 = 24$ and $3 \times 12 = 36$, so jumps of $3$ reach both. Yes, $3$ is a common factor.
3. $(c)$: $4 \times 6 = 24$ and $4 \times 9 = 36$, so jumps of $4$ reach both. Yes, $4$ is a common factor.
[Image: Let us do: Ans2: solution]
4. $(d)$: jumps of $6$ reach both, because $6 \times 4 = 24$ and $6 \times 6 = 36$, and so do jumps of $12$, because $12 \times 2 = 24$ and $12 \times 3 = 36$. Jumps of $8$ reach $24$ but not $36$, and jumps of $9$ reach $36$ but not $24$. The other jumps are $1$, $6$ and $12$.
5. $(e)$: the factors of $24$ are $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $6$, $8$, $12$, $24$. The factors of $36$ are $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $6$, $9$, $12$, $18$, $36$. In both lists: $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $6$, $12$. That is $6$ common factors.
6. $(f)$: a jump of $1$ lands on every number: $1 \times 24 = 24$ and $1 \times 36 = 36$. Yes, $1$ is a common factor of $24$ and $36$.
7. Check: $12 \times 2 = 24$ and $12 \times 3 = 36$, so $12$, the biggest common factor, reaches both.
Answer: $(a)$: Yes; $(b)$: Yes; $(c)$: Yes; $(d)$: $1$, $6$ and $12$; $(e)$: $6$ common factors: $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $6$, $12$; $(f)$: Yes, $1$ is a common factor.
[Image: Let us do: Ans2: solution (continued)]

2. $10$ is not a multiple of $4$: $4 \times 2 = 8$ and $4 \times 3 = 12$, so the jumps go from $8$ to $12$ and skip $10$.
3. $16 = 4 \times 4$, so a jump of $4$ reaches $16$.
4. $27$ is not a multiple of $4$: $4 \times 6 = 24$ and $4 \times 7 = 28$, so $27$ is skipped.
[Image: Let us do: Ans4: solution]
5. $36 = 4 \times 9$ and $48 = 4 \times 12$, so both can be reached. $0$ is the starting place.
6. Check: $16 \div 4 = 4$, $36 \div 4 = 9$ and $48 \div 4 = 12$, all exact.
Answer: $16$, $36$ and $48$ can be reached. $4$ is a common factor of $16$, $36$ and $48$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans4: solution (continued)]

content.publication_text: Which numbers will he touch if he jumps by $5$ steps? $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$. $5$ is a common factor of the numbers $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$.

content.text:
1. Jumps of $5$ from $0$ touch $5$, $10$, $15$, $20$, $25$, $30$, $35$, $40$, $45$, $50$, $55$ and $60$. The trail ends at $60$.
2. Friends on these numbers: $25 = 5 \times 5$ (Sher Khan), $30 = 5 \times 6$ (Baloo), $35 = 5 \times 7$ (Akela) and $50 = 5 \times 10$ (the rabbit).
3. No other friend is on a multiple of $5$: $4$, $9$, $12$, $14$, $21$, $39$ and $57$ are not.
4. So he touches $5$, $10$, $15$, ..., $60$, and $5$ is a common factor of the friends' numbers $25$, $30$, $35$ and $50$.
5. Check: $25 \div 5 = 5$ and $35 \div 5 = 7$, both exact.
Answer: He touches $5$, $10$, $15$, $20$, $25$, $30$, $35$, $40$, $45$, $50$, $55$ and $60$. $5$ is a common factor of $25$, $30$, $35$ and $50$.

tool_config.idea: Sort numbers into three overlapping circles by whether 2, 5 and 10 are factors of them, and find that no number goes in the circle for 10 only, because a number divisible by 10 is divisible by 2 and by 5.
tool_config.title: Number Sorter
tool_config.screen: A jungle pond clearing with three overlapping circles of floating lily rings, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a pink circle labelled divisible only by 2, a purple circle labelled divisible only by 5 and a blue circle labelled divisible only by 10, with the middle where all three meet labelled divisible by 2, 5 and 10. The circles are the largest thing on screen. Number cards, green leaf-shaped tags like the ones in your maths book, wait in a row along the bottom. A jump tester beside the circles has three small lights labelled 2, 5 and 10: when a card is picked up, each light turns green if a jump of that size lands exactly on the number and stays amber if it skips it, and the tool writes one line such as 45 ÷ 5 = 9, exactly. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a card into a circle or into the middle; tap a card to run the jump tester; Check, Hint, Retry (returns the cards of this card), Reset, Back and Next in the same places on every card. A card dropped in the wrong place slides back with a clue. Read-outs: how many cards are in each region, the three lights, and a card number out of 5.
feedback: Tapping a card runs the jump tester: each light turns green if a jump of that size lands exactly, and the tool writes one line such as 90 ÷ 10 = 9, exactly.

media.instructions_for_student: The student will understand how factors and multiples decide true or false statements, shared days and jump sizes, and why no number is divisible by 10 only.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Number Sorter
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S13.T13.C51.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (one tester, four stations)
- Textbook source: Chapter 13 Animal Jumps, Let Us Do questions 8 to 11. Practice values 14, 15, 20; 12, 105, 120, 18, 65, 100; 10, 20, 50, 80 (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student uses factors and multiples to test statements, find shared days, choose jump sizes and sort by 2, 5 and 10, and sees that no number is divisible by 10 only.
- Out of scope: divisibility by numbers other than 2, 5 and 10, prime numbers, three or more animals.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A jungle pond clearing from above (flat drawing). Three overlapping circles of lily rings: pink "Only by 2" on the left, purple "Only by 5" on the right, blue "Only by 10" at the bottom, and "By 2, 5 and 10" where all three meet. At the right a wooden tester post has three grey lights marked 2, 5 and 10. Along the bottom lie three green leaf-shaped cards like the book's: 14, 15, 20.
- Instruction line: "Test each card. Which lights will turn green for 14?"
- The child taps the lights they expect, then the card 14.
2. Scene and Objects
- Circles take most of the stage; places where only two circles overlap are empty. Cards are thumb-wide green tags. Tester: a tapped card turns a light green if that number divides it exactly ("20 ÷ 5 = 4, exactly"), else the light stays grey ("14 ÷ 5 is not exact").
- Statement bench (Star Challenge 1): a wooden sign with the statement, three example cards, round stamps "True" and "False".
- Hunting days (Star Challenge 2): paw-print tiles 0 to 60 in three rows, day 0 marked "Start"; lights "Sher Khan, every 3rd day" and "Bagheera, every 5th day"; a tray "They hunt together".
- Jump chooser (Star Challenge 3): a strip 0 to 35 with four houses (Kaa 21, Sher Khan 25, Baloo 30, Akela 35); jump stones 1 to 30; two house lights (part 1: Baloo, Sher Khan; part 2: Kaa, Akela); a basket "Good jumps" that takes a size only if Baloo's light is green and Sher Khan's grey, or in part 2 both green. Goal chip at the top left.
3. Main Interaction
- Sorting: tap lights to guess, tap a card to test it, drag a card into a circle. The drop is the guess; the tester then runs. A right drop locks in with a chime; a wrong drop slides back with one line.
- Bench: tap "True" or "False" (the guess); the examples flip with a test line; one that breaks the statement cracks the sign. Days: tap a tile; both lights green drops a gold paw in the tray. Jump chooser: tap a stone to test it, then drag a good one into the basket.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one that reads "Check", then "Next" when the goal chip is green.
- A guess is never marked wrong: if it differs, the strip says, for example, "You guessed the 10 light. Let us see."
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Test each card. Which lights will turn green for 14?" Goal chip: "Sort 3 cards". Setup: cards 14, 15, 20. Guess: tap the lights you expect, then the card. Result: 14 goes in "Only by 2", 15 in "Only by 5", 20 in the middle. Why: "14 ÷ 2 = 7. 15 ÷ 5 = 3. 20 ÷ 2 = 10, 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and 20 ÷ 10 = 2: all three lights are green." Help: guided, the tester writes every line.
- Activity 2 (independent). Goal line: "Sort these cards." Goal chip: "Sort 6 cards". Setup: 12, 105, 120, 18, 65, 100. Guess: the drop. Result: 12 and 18 "Only by 2"; 65 and 105 "Only by 5"; 100 and 120 in the middle. Why: "100 ÷ 10 = 10 and 120 ÷ 10 = 12, so both are divisible by 10, 2 and 5." Help: independent, tester lines only after a wrong drop.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Can any of these cards stay in the circle for 10 only?" Goal chip: "Test the circle for 10". Setup: cards 10, 20, 50, 80. Guess: tap "Some" or "None" for how many will stay; then drop each in "Only by 10". Result: every card slides back to the middle; the circle stays empty. Why: "20 ÷ 2 = 10 and 20 ÷ 5 = 4 as well, because 10 is 2 × 5. A number divisible by 10 is divisible by 2 and 5 too." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line (the book's question): "State whether the following statements are true (T) or false (F)." Goal chip: "Statements (a) to (f)". Guess: "True" or "False" for each. Statements, with the three examples on the bench: (a) "Factors of even numbers must be even." 8, 10, 12. (b) "Multiples of odd numbers cannot be even." 3, 5, 7. (c) "Factors of odd numbers cannot be even." 15, 21, 27. (d) "One of the common multiples of two consecutive numbers is their product." 4 and 5, 6 and 7, 8 and 9. (e) "The only common factor of any two consecutive numbers is 1." 8 and 9, 14 and 15, 20 and 21. (f) "0 cannot be a factor of any number." 5, 12, 30. Result: (a) False, (b) False, (c) True, (d) True, (e) True, (f) True. Why lines: (a) "12 is even, but its factor 3 is odd." (b) "3 is odd, but 3 × 2 = 6 is even." (c) "15, 21 and 27 have only odd factors." (d) "4 × 5 = 20 is a multiple of 4 and of 5." (e) "A jump bigger than 1 skips the next number." (f) "A jump of 0 steps never leaves 0." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line (the book's question): "Sher Khan, the tiger, goes hunting every 3rd day. Bagheera, the panther, goes hunting every 5th day. If both of them start on the same day, on which days will they be hunting together?" Goal chip: "Days they hunt together". Guess: the first tile tapped. The child taps days until the tray holds 15, 30, 45 and 60. Why: "They hunt together on days 15, 30, 45, 60 and so on: the common multiples of 3 and 5." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line (the book's question), part 1: "In the trail shown earlier, Sher Khan's house is on number 25 and that of Baloo the bear is on number 30. Mowgli wants to meet his friend Baloo the bear but wants to avoid Sher Khan's house. How long (in steps) could each jump be?" Goal chip: "Meet Baloo, miss Sher Khan". Guess: tap 5, 6 or 10 as a size that works. The basket ends with 2, 3, 6, 10, 15, 30. Why: "These jumps land on 30 and skip 25. 1 and 5 land on 25 too." Part 2: "What number of jumps (in steps) he could choose so that he can meet both Kaa, the snake, at 21 and Akela, the wolf, at 35?" Goal chip: "Meet Kaa and Akela". Guess: "Yes" or "No" for a jump of 5. The basket ends with 1 and 7. Why: "7 × 3 = 21 and 7 × 5 = 35. A jump of 3 skips 35." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line (the book's question): "Sort the following numbers into those that are (a) divisible by 2 only (b) divisible by 5 only (c) divisible by 10 only (d) divisible by 2, 5, and 10." Goal chip: "Sort 15 cards". Setup: the book's cards in three rows of five: 90, 22, 38, 30, 75, 45, 66, 78, 62, 40, 84, 56, 25, 95, 55. Guess: the drop. Result: 2 only: 22, 38, 66, 78, 62, 84, 56 (7); 5 only: 75, 45, 25, 95, 55 (5); 10 only: none; 2, 5 and 10: 90, 30, 40 (3); then the child taps the empty circle. Why: "10 is 2 × 5, so a number divisible by 10 is also divisible by 2 and 5. No number is divisible by 10 only." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A number is divisible by 2, 5 or 10 when that number is a factor of it. A number divisible by both 2 and 5 is divisible by 10, so the circle for 10 only stays empty.
- One example that breaks a statement shows it is false. Shared days are common multiples; jump sizes reaching two places are common factors.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the card locks in, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong: a red strip, a small shake, one friendly line; retry is free.
- Mistake: a card in "Only by 10" -> "A number divisible by 10 is also divisible by 2 and by 5, because 10 is 2 × 5. It goes in the middle." A card where two circles overlap -> "A number divisible by 2 and by 5 is divisible by 10. It goes in the middle."
- Mistake: 40 in "Only by 2" -> "40 ÷ 5 = 8, exactly, so 5 divides it too. Check the 5 light."
- Mistake: a wrong stamp -> a clue, for example (a) "Is 3 a factor of 12? Is 3 even?" (f) "Mowgli jumps 0 steps at a time. Can he leave 0?"
- Mistake: a day with one light green -> "Sher Khan hunts on day 3, but Bagheera does not." Day 0 -> "Day 0 is the day they start together. When do they hunt together again?"
- Mistake: 5 in the basket for Sher Khan -> "5 lands on 30, but it lands on 25 as well."
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) words: "What does divisible by 2 mean? 2 goes into the number exactly. Check 2, then 5, then 10." (2) visual: the tester runs on the card, tile, stone or example. (3) almost the answer: "65 ÷ 5 = 13, exactly, so the 5 light is green. 65 ÷ 2 and 65 ÷ 10 are not exact, so 65 goes in the circle for 5 only."
- Edge cases: 100 still goes in the middle.
7. Ending
- Each star challenge is done when its result is on screen.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A number divisible by 10 is also divisible by 2 and by 5." "One example that breaks a statement shows it is false." "Shared days are common multiples. Jumps that reach two places are common factors." Think and talk: "Why is the circle for 10 only empty? Can you find a number that belongs there?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: jungle pond clearing; lily-ring circles; green leaf-shaped cards (code-drawn); wooden tester post, sign, stamps; paw-print tiles; trail strip with four houses; Mowgli, Sher Khan, Bagheera, Baloo, Kaa, Akela (flat drawings). Language: English.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a friend says that every multiple of 5 ends in 5. Is that always true? Try 5, 10, 15 and 20. 5 and 15 end in 5, but 10 and 20 end in 0. One example that fails is enough to show that the statement is false. To show that a statement is true for every number, a few examples are not enough. Look for the reason that it always works. A reason for a true statement: every multiple of 10 is a multiple of 5, because 10 = 5 × 2, so each 10 is made of two 5s. Rule: one example that fails shows that a statement is false. To call a statement true, give the reason it always works. 1. (1): write some multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. Each one is also a multiple of 2: 2 × 2 = 4, 2 × 4 = 8, 2 × 6 = 12, 2 × 8 = 16 and 2 × 10 = 20. 2. Why it always works: 4 = 2 × 2, so every multiple of 4 is made of 2s. Statement (1) is true. 3. (2): write some multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. 12 and 24 are multiples of 4, because 4 × 3 = 12 and 4 × 6 = 24, but 6 is not: 4 × 1 = 4 and 4 × 2 = 8. 4. One multiple of 6 that is not a multiple of 4 is enough. 6 is one, so statement (2) is false. 5. Check: 18 is another example. 4 × 4 = 16 and 4 × 5 = 20, so 18 is not a multiple of 4. Answer: (1) is true because 4 = 2 × 2. (2) is false: 6 is a multiple of 6 but not of 4

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: is 60 divisible by 2? By 5? By 10? And is 35 divisible by 10? A number is divisible by 2 when 2 divides it completely, that is, when 2 is a factor of it. The same is true for 5 and for 10. 60 ÷ 2 = 30, 60 ÷ 5 = 12 and 60 ÷ 10 = 6, so 60 is divisible by 2, by 5 and by 10. 35 ÷ 5 = 7, but 35 is not divisible by 2 or by 10, so 35 is divisible by 5 only. A number divisible by 10 is always divisible by 2 and by 5, because 10 = 2 × 5: each 10 is made of five 2s and of two 5s. A number divisible by both 2 and 5 is a common multiple of 2 and 5, so it is a multiple of 10: 10, 20, 30, and so on. So no number is divisible by 10 only. Rule: check 2, 5 and 10 one by one. A number divisible by 10 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10. 1. 16: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 exactly. 5 × 3 = 15 and 5 × 4 = 20, so 16 is not divisible by 5. 16 is divisible by 2 only. 2. 35: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 exactly. 2 × 17 = 34 and 2 × 18 = 36, so 35 is not divisible by 2. 35 is divisible by 5 only. 3. 60: 60 ÷ 2 = 30, 60 ÷ 5 = 12 and 60 ÷ 10 = 6, all exact. 60 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10. 4. 48: 48 ÷ 2 = 24 exactly. 5 × 9 = 45 and 5 × 10 = 50, so 48 is not divisible by 5. 48 is divisible by 2 only. 5. 85: 85 ÷ 5 = 17 exactly. 2 × 42 = 84 and 2 × 43 = 86, so 85 is not divisible by 2. 85 is divisible by 5 only. 6. 70: 70 ÷ 2 = 35, 70 ÷ 5 = 14 and 70 ÷ 10 = 7, all exact. 70 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10. 7. No number is divisible by 10 only: 60 and 70 are divisible by 10, and both are also divisible by 2 and 5. Answer: 2 only: 16 and 48. 5 only: 35 and 85. 2, 5 and 10: 60 and 70. None is divisible by 10 only

topics.summary: A statement is false if one example breaks it, and true only if there is a reason it always works. A number is divisible by 2, 5 or 10 when that number is one of its factors.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a friend says that every multiple of 5 ends in 5. Is that always true? Try 5, 10, 15 and 20.
2. 5 and 15 end in 5, but 10 and 20 end in 0. One example that fails is enough to show that the statement is false.
3. To show that a statement is true for every number, a few examples are not enough. Look for the reason that it always works.
4. A reason for a true statement: every multiple of 10 is a multiple of 5, because 10 = 5 × 2, so each 10 is made of two 5s.
5. Rule: one example that fails shows that a statement is false. To call a statement true, give the reason it always works.

5. Rule: one example that fails shows that a statement is false. To call a statement true, give the reason it always works.

content.text:
Worked example: Check two statements. (1) Every multiple of 4 is also a multiple of 2. (2) Every multiple of 6 is also a multiple of 4.
1. (1): write some multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. Each one is also a multiple of 2: 2 × 2 = 4, 2 × 4 = 8, 2 × 6 = 12, 2 × 8 = 16 and 2 × 10 = 20.
2. Why it always works: 4 = 2 × 2, so every multiple of 4 is made of 2s. Statement (1) is true.
3. (2): write some multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. 12 and 24 are multiples of 4, because 4 × 3 = 12 and 4 × 6 = 24, but 6 is not: 4 × 1 = 4 and 4 × 2 = 8.
4. One multiple of 6 that is not a multiple of 4 is enough. 6 is one, so statement (2) is false.
5. Check: 18 is another example. 4 × 4 = 16 and 4 × 5 = 20, so 18 is not a multiple of 4.
Answer: (1) is true because 4 = 2 × 2. (2) is false: 6 is a multiple of 6 but not of 4

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 60 divisible by 2? By 5? By 10? And is 35 divisible by 10?
2. A number is divisible by 2 when 2 divides it completely, that is, when 2 is a factor of it. The same is true for 5 and for 10.
3. 60 ÷ 2 = 30, 60 ÷ 5 = 12 and 60 ÷ 10 = 6, so 60 is divisible by 2, by 5 and by 10. 35 ÷ 5 = 7, but 35 is not divisible by 2 or by 10, so 35 is divisible by 5 only.
4. A number divisible by 10 is always divisible by 2 and by 5, because 10 = 2 × 5: each 10 is made of five 2s and of two 5s.
5. A number divisible by both 2 and 5 is a common multiple of 2 and 5, so it is a multiple of 10: 10, 20, 30, and so on. So no number is divisible by 10 only.
6. Rule: check 2, 5 and 10 one by one. A number divisible by 10 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10.

content.text:
Worked example: Sort the numbers 16, 35, 60, 48, 85 and 70 into: divisible by 2 only, divisible by 5 only, and divisible by 2, 5 and 10.
1. 16: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 exactly. 5 × 3 = 15 and 5 × 4 = 20, so 16 is not divisible by 5. 16 is divisible by 2 only.
2. 35: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 exactly. 2 × 17 = 34 and 2 × 18 = 36, so 35 is not divisible by 2. 35 is divisible by 5 only.
3. 60: 60 ÷ 2 = 30, 60 ÷ 5 = 12 and 60 ÷ 10 = 6, all exact. 60 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10.
4. 48: 48 ÷ 2 = 24 exactly. 5 × 9 = 45 and 5 × 10 = 50, so 48 is not divisible by 5. 48 is divisible by 2 only.
5. 85: 85 ÷ 5 = 17 exactly. 2 × 42 = 84 and 2 × 43 = 86, so 85 is not divisible by 2. 85 is divisible by 5 only.
6. 70: 70 ÷ 2 = 35, 70 ÷ 5 = 14 and 70 ÷ 10 = 7, all exact. 70 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10.
7. No number is divisible by 10 only: 60 and 70 are divisible by 10, and both are also divisible by 2 and 5.
Answer: 2 only: 16 and 48. 5 only: 35 and 85. 2, 5 and 10: 60 and 70. None is divisible by 10 only

media.teaching_notes: 1. (a): False. 12 is even, and 3 is a factor of 12 (3 × 4 = 12), but 3 is odd. 1 is also an odd factor of every even number. 2. (b): False. 3 is odd, and 3 × 2 = 6 is a multiple of 3 that is even. 3. (c): True. If an even number were a factor of an odd number, the odd number would be a multiple of an even number, and every multiple of an even number is even. The factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5, 15 and of 21 are 1, 3, 7, 21: all odd. 4. (d): True. Take 4 and 5: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 is a multiple of 4 and of 5. Take 8 and 9: 8 × 9 = 72, a multiple of both. A product is always a multiple of the numbers multiplied. 5. (e): True. The factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4, 8 and of 9 are 1, 3, 9: only 1 is common. The factors of 14 are 1, 2, 7, 14 and of 15 are 1, 3, 5, 15: only 1 is common. A jump bigger than 1 lands on a number and then at least 2 steps further, so it cannot land on both a number and the next number. 6. (f): True. A jump of 0 steps stays at 0 for ever, so it can never reach a number. 0 × any number is 0, so 0 only makes the number 0. 7. Check: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so 3 does divide 12, and 3 × 2 = 6 is even. Answer: (a): F; (b): F; (c): T; (d): T; (e): T; (f): T

content.publication_text: State whether the following statements are true (T) or false (F). $(a)$: Factors of even numbers must be even. $(b)$: Multiples of odd numbers cannot be even. $(c)$: Factors of odd numbers cannot be even. $(d)$: One of the common multiples of two consecutive numbers is their product. $(e)$: The only common factor of any two consecutive numbers is $1$. $(f)$: $0$ cannot be a factor of any number.

content.text:
1. $(a)$: False. $12$ is even, and $3$ is a factor of $12$, because $3 \times 4 = 12$, but $3$ is odd. $1$ is also an odd factor of every even number.
2. $(b)$: False. $3$ is odd, and $3 \times 2 = 6$ is a multiple of $3$ that is even.
3. $(c)$: True. If an even number were a factor of an odd number, the odd number would be a multiple of an even number, and every multiple of an even number is even. The factors of $15$ are $1$, $3$, $5$, $15$ and of $21$ are $1$, $3$, $7$, $21$: all odd.
4. $(d)$: True. Take $4$ and $5$: $4 \times 5 = 20$, and $20$ is a multiple of $4$ and of $5$. Take $8$ and $9$: $8 \times 9 = 72$, a multiple of both. A product is always a multiple of the numbers multiplied.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
5. $(e)$: True. The factors of $8$ are $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$ and of $9$ are $1$, $3$, $9$: only $1$ is common. The factors of $14$ are $1$, $2$, $7$, $14$ and of $15$ are $1$, $3$, $5$, $15$: only $1$ is common. A jump bigger than $1$ lands on a number and then at least $2$ steps further, so it cannot land on both a number and the next number.
6. $(f)$: True. A jump of $0$ steps stays at $0$ for ever, so it can never reach a number. $0 \times$ any number is $0$, so $0$ only makes the number $0$.
7. Check: $12 \div 3 = 4$, so $3$ does divide $12$, and $3 \times 2 = 6$ is even.
Answer: $(a)$: False; $(b)$: False; $(c)$: True; $(d)$: True; $(e)$: True; $(f)$: True
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

(b): False. 3 is odd, and 3 × 2 = 6 is a multiple of 3 that is even.

(c): True. If an even number were a factor of an odd number, the odd number would be a multiple of an even number, and every multiple of an even number is even. The factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5, 15 and of 21 are 1, 3, 7, 21: all odd.
(d): True. Take 4 and 5: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 is a multiple of 4 and of 5. Take 8 and 9: 8 × 9 = 72, a multiple of both. A product is always a multiple of the numbers multiplied.

content.text: Sher Khan, the tiger, goes hunting every $3\text{rd}$ day. Bagheera, the panther, goes hunting every $5\text{th}$ day. If both of them start on the same day, on which days will they be hunting together?

content.publication_text: Sher Khan, the tiger, goes hunting every $3\text{rd}$ day. Bagheera, the panther, goes hunting every $5\text{th}$ day. If both of them start on the same day, on which days will they be hunting together?

content.text:
1. Count the day they start together as day $0$, like the start of a number line.
2. Sher Khan hunts on days $3$, $6$, $9$, $12$, $15$, $18$, $21$, $24$, $27$, $30$, and so on: the multiples of $3$.
3. Bagheera hunts on days $5$, $10$, $15$, $20$, $25$, $30$, and so on: the multiples of $5$.
4. Both hunt on days $15$, $30$, $45$ and so on. These are the common multiples of $3$ and $5$, and the first is day $15$, because $3 \times 5 = 15$.
5. Check: $3 \times 10 = 30$ and $5 \times 6 = 30$; $3 \times 15 = 45$ and $5 \times 9 = 45$.
Answer: On days $15$, $30$, $45$, $60$ and so on, the common multiples of $3$ and $5$, after the day they start together.

content.text:
1. $(a)$: a jump meets Baloo at $30$ when the jump size is a factor of $30$. The factors of $30$ are $1$, $2$, $3$, $5$, $6$, $10$, $15$, $30$.
2. A jump avoids Sher Khan at $25$ when the jump size is not a factor of $25$. The factors of $25$ are $1$, $5$, $25$.
3. Take out the jump sizes that land on $25$: $1$, because $1 \times 25 = 25$, and $5$, because $5 \times 5 = 25$.
4. The jumps that meet Baloo and avoid Sher Khan are $2$, $3$, $6$, $10$, $15$ and $30$ steps.
[Image: Let us do: Ans3: solution]
5. $(b)$: the jump must be a common factor of $21$ and $35$. The factors of $21$ are $1$, $3$, $7$, $21$ and of $35$ are $1$, $5$, $7$, $35$. Common: $1$ and $7$.
6. Check: $7 \times 3 = 21$ and $7 \times 5 = 35$. Also $6 \times 5 = 30$, and jumps of $6$ go $24$ then $30$, skipping $25$.
Answer: $(a)$: $2$, $3$, $6$, $10$, $15$ or $30$ steps. $(b)$: $1$ or $7$ steps.
[Image: Let us do: Ans3: solution (continued)]

A jump avoids Sher Khan at 25 when the jump size is not a factor of 25. The factors of 25 are 1, 5, 25.
Take out the jump sizes that land on 25: 1, because 1 × 25 = 25, and 5, because 5 × 5 = 25.
The jumps that meet Baloo and avoid Sher Khan are 2, 3, 6, 10, 15 and 30 steps.
(b): the jump must be a common factor of 21 and 35. The factors of 21 are 1, 3, 7, 21 and of 35 are 1, 5, 7, 35. Common: 1 and 7.
Check: 7 × 3 = 21 and 7 × 5 = 35. Also 6 × 5 = 30, and jumps of 6 go 24 then 30, skipping 25.
content.answer: (a): 2, 3, 6, 10, 15 or 30 steps. (b): 1 or 7 steps.

content.publication_text: Sort the following numbers into those that are $(a)$: divisible by $2$ only $(b)$: divisible by $5$ only $(c)$: divisible by $10$ only $(d)$: divisible by $2$, $5$, and $10$. $90$, $22$, $38$, $30$, $75$, $45$, $66$, $78$, $62$, $40$, $84$, $56$, $25$, $95$, $55$

content.text:
1. A number is divisible by $2$ when $2$ is a factor of it. The same is true for $5$ and for $10$.
2. $90$: $90 \div 2 = 45$, $90 \div 5 = 18$ and $90 \div 10 = 9$, all exact. $90$ is divisible by $2$, $5$ and $10$.
3. $30$: $30 \div 2 = 15$, $30 \div 5 = 6$ and $30 \div 10 = 3$. $40$: $40 \div 2 = 20$, $40 \div 5 = 8$ and $40 \div 10 = 4$. All exact, so $30$ and $40$ are divisible by $2$, $5$ and $10$ too.
[Image: Let us do: Ans4: solution]
4. $22$, $38$, $66$, $78$, $62$, $84$ and $56$ are divisible by $2$ but not by $5$ (for example $22 \div 2 = 11$, but $5 \times 4 = 20$ and $5 \times 5 = 25$ skip $22$). So these $7$ are divisible by $2$ only.
5. $75$, $45$, $25$, $95$ and $55$ are divisible by $5$ but not by $2$, because they are odd (for example $45 \div 5 = 9$). So these $5$ are divisible by $5$ only.
6. No number is divisible by $10$ only: a number divisible by $10$ is also divisible by $2$ and $5 (10 = 2 \times 5)$, so $90$, $30$ and $40$ go in the middle.
7. Check: $7 + 5 + 3 = 15$, the same as the number of cards.
Answer: $(a)$: $22$, $38$, $66$, $78$, $62$, $84$, $56$; $(b)$: $75$, $45$, $25$, $95$, $55$; $(c)$: none; $(d)$: $90$, $30$, $40$
[Image: Let us do: Ans4: solution (continued)]
steps: A number is divisible by 2 when 2 is a factor of it. The same is true for 5 and for 10.
90: 90 ÷ 2 = 45, 90 ÷ 5 = 18 and 90 ÷ 10 = 9, all exact. 90 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10.
22, 38, 66, 78, 62, 84 and 56 are divisible by 2 but not by 5 (for example 22 ÷ 2 = 11, but 5 × 4 = 20 and 5 × 5 = 25 skip 22). So these 7 are divisible by 2 only.
75, 45, 25, 95 and 55 are divisible by 5 but not by 2, because they are odd (for example 45 ÷ 5 = 9). So these 5 are divisible by 5 only.
No number is divisible by 10 only: a number divisible by 10 is also divisible by 2 and 5 (10 = 2 × 5), so 90, 30 and 40 go in the middle.
Check: 7 + 5 + 3 = 15, the same as the number of cards.

topics.summary: The chapter's ideas in one walk along the trail: factors and multiples, arrays, prime numbers, common multiples, common factors, testing statements, and using them for the hunting days and the trail.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have jumped along the whole trail. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the hidden box to the hunting days? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Factors and multiples: a number you multiply by is a factor of the answer, and the answer is a multiple of it. The box that gave 28, 36, 48 and 72 could multiply by 1, 2 or 4, the common factors of the four numbers.
3. Check: 4 × 7 = 28 and 4 × 9 = 36, so 28 and 36 are multiples of 4.
4. Arrays: the arrays of a number show its factors. 12 has the arrays 1 × 12, 2 × 6 and 3 × 4, so its factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. 1 and the number itself are always factors, and a number is a multiple of each of its factors.
5. Check: what are the factors of 10? 1, 2, 5 and 10, from the arrays 1 × 10 and 2 × 5.
6. Prime numbers: a number whose only array is 1 × the number has only two factors, 1 and itself. 13 and 37 are prime numbers.
7. Check: is 14 a prime number? No, 14 has the factors 1, 2, 7 and 14.
8. Common multiples: the numbers two jumpers both touch. 3 and 4 have the common multiples 12, 24, 36, and so on, the multiples of the first one, 12.
9. Check: what are the first three common multiples of 4 and 6? 12, 24 and 36.
10. Common factors: the jump sizes that land on every number of a list. The common factors of 24 and 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. 1 is always a common factor, and 12 and 13 have only 1.
11. Check: which jump sizes reach both 8 and 12? Jumps of 1, 2 and 4.
12. Testing statements: one example that fails shows a statement is false. A multiple of an odd number can be even, as in 3 × 2 = 6. A number divisible by 10 is divisible by 2 and by 5.
13. Check: is every factor of an even number even? No, 3 is a factor of 12.
14. Using the ideas: Sher Khan hunts every 3rd day and Bagheera every 5th day, so they hunt together on days 15, 30, 45 and so on. Mowgli can meet Baloo at 30 and avoid Sher Khan at 25 with jumps of 2, 3, 6, 10, 15 or 30 steps.

modules.module_summary: Testing statements about factors and multiples, sorting numbers by the factors 2, 5 and 10, using common multiples and common factors for the hunting days and the trail, and a revision of the whole chapter.

objectives.objective_text: Students find the numbers a box could multiply by to make a list of numbers, and name these multipliers as factors and the numbers that come out as multiples of them.
Students find the multipliers that fit the numbers coming out of the box, and say which numbers could have gone in for each multiplier.
Students make every array of a number with square tiles, write each array as a multiplication, and list all the factors of the number.
Students show that a number is a multiple of each of its factors, including 1 and the number itself, by writing the multiplications that make the number.
Students decide whether a number has only one array by trying every number of rows, and name a number with only two factors a prime number.
Students make the arrays of a number, list its factors, and explain why a number such as 13 or 37 has only two factors.
Students find the numbers two jumpers both touch on a number line, name them common multiples, and say which one is the first common multiple.
Students describe the pattern of the common multiples of two numbers and use the first common multiple to write the next ones.
Students find common multiples of pairs of numbers by jumping and by lists, and decide which animal lands on a number at the end of the road.
Students decide whether a jump size lands exactly on a number, and say that it does when the jump size is a factor of that number.
Students list the factors of two numbers, pick the common factors, and say which jump sizes reach both numbers.
Students find which friends a jump size reaches on the trail, and list the common factors of two numbers and of pairs of numbers.
Students decide whether a statement about factors and multiples is true or false by testing it on examples, and give an example that makes a false statement fail.
Students tell whether a number is divisible by 2, by 5 and by 10 by checking which of these are its factors, and explain why a number divisible by 10 is divisible by 2 and 5.
Students use factors, multiples and common multiples to decide true or false statements, find hunting days, choose jump sizes on the trail, and sort numbers by 2, 5 and 10.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Numbers put in this box get multiplied by a number and come out. Four numbers come out of the box: 28, 36, 48 and 72. (a): Can you guess the multiplier if you see the 4 numbers coming out of the box? (b): Is there more than one possible multiplier? (c): What numbers might have been put inside the box? Share your thoughts in the class.
Book item: A number, when arranged in an array, shows the factors of that number. Are there other numbers that are factors of 15? Try to make other arrays for the number 15.
Book item: Make different arrays for the following numbers. Identify the factors in each case. (a): 10; (b): 14; (c): 13; (d): 20; (e): 25; (f): 32; (g): 37; (h): 46; (i): 54
Book item: Numbers like 13 and 37 are called prime numbers. Why?
Book item: 12 is the first common multiple of 3 and 4. What are some other common multiples of 3 and 4? You can continue the number line or take help from the times tables of 3 and 4.
Book item: Let us write the multiples of two numbers, 4 and 6. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, ... Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, ... 12 and 24 are two of the common multiples of 4 and 6. List a few more.
Book item: Find 5 common multiples of the following pairs of numbers. (a): 2 and 3; (b): 5 and 8; (c): 2 and 4; (d): 3 and 9; (e): 5 and 10; (f): 9 and 12; (g): 8 and 12; (h): 6 and 8; (i): 6 and 9

Book item: Food is available at the end of a cobbled road. Robby, the rabbit, takes a jump of 4 each time. Deeku, the deer, takes a jump of 6 each time. They both start at 0. Will both Robby and Deeku reach the food? Who will reach first? How do you know? Explain your answer.
Book item: Mowgli's friends live along the trail on the marked places below. Which of his friends will he be able to visit, if he jumps by 2 steps starting from 0?
Book item: Which of his friends will he be able to meet if he jumps by 3 steps? 3 is a common factor of the numbers ___.
Book item: Which numbers will he touch if he jumps by 5 steps? ___. 5 is a common factor of the numbers ___.
Book item: Which numbers will he touch if he jumps by 10 steps? ___. 10 is a common factor of the numbers ___.

Book item: Let us find some common factors of the numbers 24 and 36. Note that all jumps in the following questions start from 0. (a): Can we jump by 2 steps at a time to reach both 24 and 36? Yes/No. 2 is/is not a common factor of 24 and 36. (b): Can we jump by 3 steps at a time to reach both 24 and 36? Yes/No. 3 is/is not a common factor of 24 and 36. (c): Can we jump by 4 steps at a time to reach both 24 and 36? Yes/No. 4 is/is not a common factor of 24 and 36. (d): What other jumps can we take to reach both 24 and 36? (e): How many common factors can you find for 24 and 36? List them. (f): What about jumping by 1 step each time to reach both 24 and 36?
Book item: What are the common factors of 12 and 13?
Book item: Find which of the following numbers can be reached by jumps of 4 steps? 4 is the common factor of the numbers ___.

Book item: Find the common factors of the following pairs of numbers. (a): 12 and 16; (b): 8 and 12; (c): 4 and 16; (d): 2 and 9; (e): 3 and 5; (f): 12 and 15; (g): 20 and 5; (h): 9 and 21; (i): 6 and 27

Book item: State whether the following statements are true (T) or false (F). (a): Factors of even numbers must be even. (b): Multiples of odd numbers cannot be even. (c): Factors of odd numbers cannot be even. (d): One of the common multiples of two consecutive numbers is their product. (e): The only common factor of any two consecutive numbers is 1. (f): 0 cannot be a factor of any number.
Book item: Sher Khan, the tiger, goes hunting every 3rd day. Bagheera, the panther, goes hunting every 5th day. If both of them start on the same day, on which days will they be hunting together?

Book item: (a): In the trail shown earlier, Sher Khan's house is on number 25 and that of Baloo the bear is on number 30. Mowgli wants to meet his friend Baloo the bear but wants to avoid Sher Khan's house. How long (in steps) could each jump be? (b): What number of jumps (in steps) he could choose so that he can meet both Kaa, the snake, at 21 and Akela, the wolf, at 35?

Book item: Sort the following numbers into those that are (a): divisible by 2 only (b): divisible by 5 only (c): divisible by 10 only (d): divisible by 2, 5, and 10. 90, 22, 38, 30, 75, 45, 66, 78, 62, 40, 84, 56, 25, 95, 55

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place in the jungle trail of Mowgli and his animal friends. Animals jump along a number line from 0, and where they land shows what factors, multiples, common multiples and common factors are. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Five tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.
points.title: Videos teach, tools explore

points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own questions, used exactly as the book gives them.
points.title: A tool in three steps

points.text: Every answerable prompt and every Let Us Do question of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.
points.title: Every book question has its own video

points.text: Arrays of square tiles, number lines with animal jumps, the numbered trail and the three circles for sorting carry each idea, with the numbers large and clear.
points.title: The picture is the mathematics

points.text: The box numbers, the trail and its friends, the cobbled road and every question are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.
points.title: Only the book's numbers
